name: Ringo Corponation Drift Mesh Node
description: The Ringo Corponation Drift Mesh Node is a compact, autonomous wireless relay unit designed to be deployed in environments where conventional fixed-infrastructure communication is unavailable, compromised, or under active surveillance. Roughly the size and weight of a large coin, the Drift Node adheres to any surface via micro-suction backing and immediately begins broadcasting a localized mesh relay point that integrates with other Drift Nodes and compatible devices in range, self-organizing into an encrypted peer-to-peer network without any central routing infrastructure. Up to sixty-four nodes can form a single self-healing mesh, automatically rerouting traffic around destroyed or compromised nodes within milliseconds.

specifications.mesh_capacity: Up to 64 nodes per self-organizing network
specifications.transmission_signature: Mimics urban IoT device traffic (utility meters, environmental sensors)
specifications.memory_wipe: Automatic at 24-hour mark or on tamper detection
specifications.housing_degradation: Full biodegradation within 14 days of deployment

tactical_use: Operators seed Drift Nodes throughout a target area in advance of an operation — tucked behind pipes, pressed under window ledges, stuck to the undersides of furniture. The resulting mesh provides a private communication infrastructure that exists entirely within the operational zone, immune to the target facility's own jamming or monitoring systems because it runs on frequencies that appear to be the building's own IoT backbone. Teams use the mesh for real-time coordination, triggering remote devices, and maintaining communication in structures designed to suppress external signals. Post-operation, the nodes are left in place to degrade naturally.
cultural_context: The Drift Node's legal status and low cost have made it ubiquitous across every tier of Meridian 88's society. Street vendors sell them openly alongside legitimate tech accessories. Their legitimate construction-site use case is real and common enough that possession alone is meaningless as evidence of criminal intent, which is precisely why organized groups prefer them. There is a certain democratic quality to the Drift Node — it is one of the few pieces of serious operational communications hardware available to someone with very little money. Community organizers in contested districts use them to maintain neighborhood communication networks when corporate entities shut down local mesh infrastructure during labor disputes.
known_users: Legitimate construction and event management crews
Street-level fixers establishing temporary secure channels
story_hooks: The party discovers an active DriftNet mesh in a building they're sweeping — the nodes are still fresh, meaning whoever deployed them is either still present or left very recently.
A community mesh network built from Drift Nodes in a lower-city district has been quietly co-opted by someone inserting nodes running modified firmware that logs all traffic before forwarding it.

Ringo Corponation's compliance flag system has been sold wholesale to a corporate intelligence buyer — every bulk Drift Node purchase in the past eight months has been logged and cross-referenced with known dissident networks.

A Drift Node that should have wiped and degraded is still active three months after a completed operation, broadcasting on a frequency that doesn't match DriftNet protocol — something is using the hardware as a shell for a different kind of transmission.
